sm: The hosts open the Cross Politic show with the title Midterms Autopsy and welcome guest Steve Deace. They joke about whether the Republican party needs an autopsy or a resurrection. Deace says the president broke covenant with his base, and that there is always a price for that. He compares it to George H. W. Bush in 1988, whose read my lips, no new taxes pledge was followed by a major tax increase two years later. That split the Republican base, hurt the economy, and opened the door to Ross Perot, who got nineteen percent. He then starts on Bill Clinton, who won in 1992 as a new Democrat.

Deace continues the history. Clinton raised taxes and tried Hillarycare, and voters punished him in 1994, but he reinvented himself and won in 1996. George W. Bush was hammered in 2006 and then fought his own base, which fed the Tea Party and Barack Obama's 2008 win. Deace says that if Trump reinvents himself and lifts his approval into the mid forties, Republicans likely win in 2028 whether the nominee is Vance, DeSantis or Rubio. If not, he says, they get creamed. He adds that Republicans struggle to govern nationally because corporate interests and the base want different things. He blames passive primary voters and weak establishment endorsements, and says Trump is a disruptor, not a manager.

The hosts say the problems go beyond Trump. They point out that Republicans with the House and Senate under Bush and under Trump's first two years got little done, and that the Save Act stalled in the Senate. One host says Republicans are not simply cowards, because many do not truly share the base's convictions. They compare it to someone pitching a religion they have not internalized. They give the example of an Oklahoma senator who is personally devout yet introduced an amnesty bill. A host on the board of the Idaho Family Policy Center says many evangelical legislators have never been taught what the Bible says about government, so education is part of their work. They then ask Deace about Texas and other states.

Deace says Iowa kept both legislative chambers and made tax increases nearly impossible, even while electing a Democratic governor. Kansas elected a Democratic senator while passing a tougher Save Act style measure. He calls the election Watergate level in its rejection of a party and its leader, because Trump broke promises on accountability, affordability and foreign wars. On Texas, the hosts blame Governor Abbott, who campaigned on property taxes for twelve years. Deace says one in five early voters had skipped recent primaries. He argues that technocratic Republican managerialism lost to James Talarico, who drew millennial and Gen Z voters to a redefined Christianity, and that people will choose bad theology over none.

Deace says Ron DeSantis governed like a Christian conservative, did what he promised, and grew his base by about twenty points, while Abbott's vote stayed flat. He says much of the party would rather lose to Democrats than lose control to people like them. He notes that challenging incumbents is easier now because many are leaving. He says Republicans are in a catch twenty-two, since the Democratic party threatens to turn states into California. He adds that young men lack the path to a house and family that earlier generations had, so they are radicalized, and that voting feels like Russian roulette. Knox then joins and asks what Deace would do if he were Trump's chief of staff.

Deace says he would replace chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, but warns Trump not to then go wobbly. He wants a credible voter fraud conviction, suggesting the Alaska case, and wants Howard Lutnick fired and someone from the Epstein list prosecuted, as acts of atonement. He says Democrats will offer only Medicare for all and taxes, so Republicans can own affordability. On free markets, he would tell Generation X to be the we'll take it generation, moving those born after 1980 off Social Security into Trump accounts so their children are free. Knox then asks for a short summary on Iran.

Deace says he detests the Iranian regime but believes Trump hoped for cheap regime change after Venezuela and the protests in Tehran. He argues nobody knew what would replace the regime, noting Kurdish ambitions, a large Shia population, and over three hundred thousand soldiers. He says the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz raised fuel prices and cost the election. Now, he says, cutting and running would be a huge propaganda win for Iran and a jihadi recruitment video. He urges the president to find a way to claim a win with a show of force. After Deace leaves, the hosts discuss the covenant imagery of animals split in two, tying a broken covenant to death.

The hosts say the autopsy is really of the people, not just the president, because voters get the leader they represent. They tie it to marriage, noting that God hates divorce, and to the reported affair of the Nvidia chief executive that they say put a nation at risk. Knox says conservatives often want their own version of fascism over the other side's and no longer believe free markets work, pointing to calls to treat wives like single moms for benefits. He says the only way to beat China is with free markets and free people. They conclude God may be showing that a covenant-breaking people gets a covenant-breaking leader, and a host begins reading First Thessalonians four.

Reading First Thessalonians four, the hosts say God is the avenger of broken covenants, and point to divorce, adultery and pornography rates. They say the first crime scene in the Nvidia story was the man's own family, and that a nation is only as healthy as its families. They say Republicans avoid real conversations about conservatism, citing Idaho officials such as Governor Brad Little, who they criticize for promoting India at a Diwali event and for COVID closures. They also mention affairs involving Ken Paxton and Russell Fulcher, and want a Bible study with such leaders. They praise DeSantis for ignoring political calculation, and say they will have to make an argument for virtue.

The hosts say the argument for virtue must come from culture, built in homes. One host describes children who honor their mother, behave in public and work alongside their parents. He says families have two jobs, glorifying God and producing something of value to trade, and that businesses run by such families gain influence without needing votes. Another says to focus on what you control, like your kids, your fidelity and your work, and mentions a Christian business network called Business Makers Network. They say the dominion mandate to Adam and Eve is how culture normally changes, with husbands working hard and wives homemaking. They end by saying children are given to be taught, citing Deuteronomy six.

The hosts say the home is the primary place where saints are grown, and that when COVID shut things down, their families asked what dad would do, not what the government would do. They argue that men who must trust God to provide for a one-income household build faith that creates wealth, and that this struggle explains why Christians have less wealth. They say the Nvidia chief executive is not an elected official yet his unfaithfulness threatens everyone. They say a man's family qualifies him to lead in church and civil office, because managing a family resembles managing a business. They close by urging single people to marry, married couples to have children and baptize them, and by signing off for Cross Politic.
